resolved_conflicts.explanation: An April 1938 newspaper item quoted by Forest Lookouts gives about 130 feet above sea level; NHLR gives 127 ft (39 m). The record keeps the NHLR figure, 38.7 m.

Each county paid $25. A 1938 newspaper says the $25 covered the land bought from Samuel Haynie and gives the investment as about $1,800; NHLR says the $25 each went toward a total cost of $1,800. The two accounts disagree on what the money bought, and the story reports both rather than choosing one.

The Rappahannock Record describes Almost in the Clouds as the story of the tower; Wikipedia says the tower was the subject of a novel by the same author. Neither source names a genre for the book, so the story reports both descriptions and does not call them a conflict.

The 1938 items name the Forest Service, a division of the Virginia Conservation Commission; NHLR names the Virginia Department of Forestry. The sources do not say when or why the name changed; the story uses the current name.

notes_for_editor: The 1938 build, design and cost rest on NHLR plus two 1938 newspaper items quoted by Forest Lookouts. Staffing and the fire history rest on NHLR alone; no source read names a fire the tower spotted or staffing after the 1980s. The Rappahannock Record article is paywalled, so only its lead was read. The book by Anthony-Tolbert was not read and may fill the gaps. The seasonal staffing value describes the historical pattern, not current staffing. The brief record checks out (height 30.5 m, elevation 38.7 m from 127 ft, the 1938 and 2026 events), so no corrections. No new photos: NHLR credits a photo to Susan Anthony-Tolbert but gives no image URL. The April 1938 clipping spells the chairman's name 'Wolbur' and the June item spells it 'Wilbur'. Not verified: current condition beyond the Forest Fire Lookout Association standing listing.
